questiontext.text: At each step, Huffman's algorithm merges which two nodes?

answer.text: The two nodes with the lowest frequencies

feedback.text: Correct — greedily merge the two smallest, giving the merged node their combined frequency.

answer.text: The two nodes with the highest frequencies

feedback.text: No — merging the largest first would give frequent symbols longer codes.

answer.text: Any two adjacent nodes in the input order

feedback.text: No — the choice is by frequency, not position.

answer.text: The node with the highest and the node with the lowest frequency

feedback.text: No — always the two lowest are combined.

generalfeedback.text: Huffman is greedy: repeatedly extract the two lowest-frequency nodes from a min-heap and merge them into a parent whose frequency is their sum.

questiontext.text: What key property of a Huffman code makes decoding unambiguous?

answer.text: No codeword is a prefix of another codeword

feedback.text: Correct — this prefix-free property lets a decoder split the bitstream unambiguously.

answer.text: All codewords have the same length

feedback.text: No — Huffman codes are variable length; that describes a fixed-length code.

answer.text: Codewords are assigned in alphabetical order

feedback.text: No — assignment is driven by frequency, not alphabet.

answer.text: Every codeword starts with a 0 bit

feedback.text: No — that is not a property of Huffman codes.

generalfeedback.text: Because symbols sit only at leaves of the tree, no codeword is a prefix of another, so the decoder never needs lookahead.

questiontext.text: In a Huffman code, symbols that appear more frequently receive codewords that are:

answer.text: Shorter

feedback.text: Correct — frequent symbols land near the root, giving shorter codes and minimizing total length.

answer.text: Longer

feedback.text: No — that would increase the encoded size.

answer.text: The same length as every other symbol

feedback.text: No — that is a fixed-length code, not Huffman.

answer.text: Always exactly one bit

feedback.text: No — only possible with two or fewer symbols.

generalfeedback.text: Assigning shorter codewords to more frequent symbols minimizes the expected number of bits, producing a minimum-redundancy code.

questiontext.text: Using a min-heap (priority queue), what is the time to build a Huffman tree for n symbols?

answer.text: O(n log n)

feedback.text: Correct — n-1 merges, each with O(log n) heap operations.

answer.text: O(n)

feedback.text: No — heap operations add a log n factor unless frequencies are pre-sorted.
No — a naive linear scan for the minimum would give this, but a heap is faster.
No — the construction is not exponential.

generalfeedback.text: There are n-1 merges; each extract-min and insert costs O(log n), so the total is O(n log n).

questiontext.text: Huffman coding produces an optimal (minimum-length) prefix code for a given set of symbol frequencies.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — it is optimal among symbol-by-symbol prefix codes.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: It is provably optimal for per-symbol prefix codes.

questiontext.text: Huffman's algorithm requires dynamic programming to decide which nodes to merge.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: No — it is a greedy algorithm; the local choice of the two smallest is provably globally optimal.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — Huffman is greedy, not dynamic programming.

questiontext.text: A code in which no codeword is a prefix of another is called a ______-free code.

answer.text: prefix

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: prefix*

feedback.text: Correct.

questiontext.text: Which statements about Huffman coding are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: It uses a min-heap to repeatedly extract the two lowest-frequency nodes

feedback.text: Yes — that is the core of the greedy construction.

answer.text: Symbols are stored only at the leaves of the tree

feedback.text: Yes — internal nodes are merged frequency sums, not symbols.

answer.text: All symbols get codewords of equal length

feedback.text: No — Huffman codes are variable length.

answer.text: The merged node's frequency is the product of its children's frequencies

feedback.text: No — it is the sum, not the product.

generalfeedback.text: Huffman: min-heap driven greedy merges of the two smallest, symbols at leaves, variable-length codewords, merged frequency = sum of children.
